raw_case_text: A 5 1/2-year-old HIV-infected boy presented with recurrent fever and cough since 2 years, recurrent diarrhea and vomiting since 6 months and generalized pruritis and abdominal pain since 15 days. He had taken ATT 2 years ago for 6 months. His father was a prisoner and was diagnosed to be HIV-infected 2 years back. His mother was also diagnosed to be HIV infected a year back. Thus, the child seemed to have acquired the HIV infection vertically. He was immunized till date. On examination, he was malnourished (weight=10 kg, <5th centile and height=96 cm, <5th centile). He had pallor, multiple mobile nontender cervical, axillary and inguinal lymphnodes with oral thrush. On systemic examination, he had mild splenomegaly. Other systems were normal. His investigations showed hemoglobin of 11.4 g/dl, white cell count of 7,200/mm3 and ESR of 62 mm at end of 1 h. X-ray chest showed bilateral hilar congestion. Mantoux test was negative. Liver function and renal function tests were normal. His enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for HIV was repeated, which was positive. A baseline CD4 count of 161 cells/mm3 was detected, with a CD4 percentage of 7.98%, suggestive of severe immunosuppression. He was started on three drugs; ART consisting of Stavudine, Lamivudine and Efavirenz. He had a weight gain of 2 kg within 1 month of starting ART and his lymphadenopathy regressed. However, his cough and pruritis persisted. A repeat X-ray chest showed a right-sided lower zone pneumonia. A Mantoux test performed at this time was negative. He was treated with antibiotics but the pneumonia did not subside, and thus he was started on ATT to which the pneumonia responded. Three months after start of ATT, he developed left cervical matted rubbery lymphadenopathy (4 cmx4 cm) that did not subside with antibiotics. Fine needle aspiration of the cervical adenopathy was carried out, which showed caseous granulomas. Drug compliance with ATT was confirmed. A wedge biopsy of the node was carried out, which again confirmed tuberculosis, and then the child was started on six-drug ATT. Subsequently, within 1 week, he developed severe sepsis with intestinal obstruction and was hospitalized. CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed multiple splenic lesions, a large liver lesion, encasing retroperitoneal lymphnodes, large right pelvic lymphnodes and a large right inguinal lymphnode with a large presacral mass (6.8 cmx5.08 cm) with intrasacral extension into the spinal cord suggestive of lymphoma [Figure 2]. However, before any intervention could be started, the child expired the following day. A postmortem lymph node biopsy was performed, which showed round cell tumor that was found to be a B cell lymphoma on immunophenotyping.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5.5-year-old HIV-positive boy presented with a 2-year history of recurrent fever and cough, a 6-month history of recurrent diarrhea and vomiting, and a 15-day history of generalized pruritus and abdominal pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The child experienced recurrent fevers and cough for 2 years (having completed a 6-month course of anti-tuberculosis therapy 2 years earlier), recurrent diarrhea and emesis for 6 months, and generalized pruritus and abdominal pain for 15 days prior to presentation.
subjective.past_medical_history: Vertically acquired HIV infection (father was a prisoner diagnosed with HIV 2 years prior; mother diagnosed with HIV 1 year prior); completed a 6-month course of anti-tuberculosis therapy (ATT) 2 years prior; immunizations up to date.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent fever, cough, diarrhea, vomiting, generalized pruritus, abdominal pain, and severe failure to thrive.

objective.physical_examination: Severely malnourished (weight 10 kg [<5th percentile], height 96 cm [<5th percentile]) with pallor, oral thrush, multiple mobile non-tender cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes, and mild splenomegaly. Three months after restarting ATT on ART, he developed a 4 x 4 cm matted rubbery left cervical lymphadenopathy.
objective.routine_investigations: Baseline labs showed hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, WBC 7,200/mm3, elevated ESR (62 mm at 1 hour), normal liver and renal function tests, negative Mantoux tuberculin skin test (at baseline and repeat), and positive repeat HIV ELISA. Baseline chest X-ray showed bilateral hilar congestion; repeat chest X-ray at 1 month showed right lower zone consolidation/pneumonia.
objective.advanced_workup: Baseline CD4+ T-cell count was 161 cells/mm3 (CD4% = 7.98%). Fine-needle aspiration and wedge biopsy of the 4 x 4 cm matted left cervical lymph node confirmed caseous necrotizing tuberculous granulomas. Subsequent abdominal and pelvic CT (performed during acute decompensation with sepsis and intestinal obstruction) revealed multiple splenic lesions, a large hepatic mass, encasing retroperitoneal, right pelvic, and right inguinal lymphadenopathy, and a 6.8 x 5.08 cm presacral mass with intrasacral spinal canal extension. Postmortem lymph node biopsy and immunophenotyping confirmed B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Vertically acquired pediatric HIV/AIDS (confirmed by positive HIV ELISA, baseline CD4+ count 161 cells/mm3 [7.98%]) complicated by pulmonary and paradoxical/unmasking cervical lymph node tuberculosis and rapidly fatal high-grade intra-abdominal/presacral B-cell lymphoma. Following initiation of triple antiretroviral therapy (stavudine, lamivudine, and efavirenz), the child gained 2 kg in the first month, was started on first-line anti-tuberculosis therapy (ATT) for antibiotic-refractory right lower lobe pneumonia, and was escalated at 3 months to six-drug ATT after biopsy confirmation of caseating cervical tuberculous lymphadenitis. One week later, he developed fulminant sepsis and acute intestinal obstruction from disseminated B-cell lymphoma (confirmed by postmortem nodal biopsy and immunophenotyping) and died the following day.
